$comment: Worked examples both sides test against.
The schema next to this file says what the payloads look like; this says what
the signed strings are, byte for byte. Two implementations in two languages
can agree on a schema and still disagree on a signature — over date
formatting, property order, or how an absent value is rendered — and a
signature that only sometimes verifies is worse than none at all.
So each sample carries a payload and the exact canonical string that must be
produced from it. KNIGHT asserts it in Knight.IntegrationTests; the reference
store asserts it in knight_integration/tests. A change to either
implementation that alters the string fails on both sides immediately.

notes: Features are sorted by slug with an ordinal comparison, so the order never
depends on a database collation or the culture the process runs in.
An absent expiry is a single hyphen, not an empty string, so it cannot be
Timestamps are Unix seconds: integers mean the same thing in both languages.
The signature itself is empty in the sample: it is what the canonical form
produces, so it cannot also be an input to it.
The path only, never the host: a proxy in front of a store may rewrite the
host, and binding the signature to it would break every store behind one.
The store accepts the signature only inside its clock-skew window, so a
captured request cannot be replayed tomorrow.
